claim: Saturn is losing ring material to the planet.
excerpt: New NASA research confirms that Saturn is losing its iconic rings at the maximum rate estimated from Voyager 1 & 2 observations made decades ago.
context: The loss is inferred from measured infrared emission, not from watching the rings shrink. Marked as a model on screen for that reason.

claim: Saturn orbits about 9.6 times farther from the Sun than Earth (1,432.0 vs 149.6 million km).
excerpt: Distance from Sun (10^6 km): Earth 149.6, Saturn 1432.0
context: Ratio 1432.0 / 149.6 = 9.57, computed from the two fact-sheet values. The narration rounds this to 'nearly ten times'.

claim: The Keck Observatory in Hawaii observed Saturn's bands in April 2011.
excerpt: with the W.M Keck Observatory on Mauna Kea, in Hawaii, in April 2011

claim: Dark bands appeared in Saturn's upper-atmosphere glow, around 25 to 55 degrees latitude.
excerpt: What they observed instead was a series of light and dark bands ... from around 25 to 55 degrees latitude
context: Observed in the infrared. The render shows the band location in visible colours so it can be seen.

claim: Ring rain: electrically charged ice particles flow from the rings along Saturn's magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere.
excerpt: proposing that electrically charged ice particles from Saturn's rings were flowing down invisible magnetic field lines, dumping water in Saturn's upper atmosphere where these lines emerged from the planet.
context: The bands are observed; the particle flow that explains them is the model.

claim: Researchers estimate ring rain drains enough water products to fill an Olympic-sized swimming pool in half an hour.
excerpt: We estimate that this 'ring rain' drains an amount of water products that could fill an Olympic-sized swimming pool from Saturn's rings in half an hour
context: A researcher's estimate from James O'Donoghue. Spoken as an estimate.

claim: With ring rain plus the inflow Cassini measured at the equator, the rings could last less than 100 million years; ring rain alone gives about 300 million.
excerpt: From this alone, the entire ring system will be gone in 300 million years, but add to this the Cassini-spacecraft measured ring-material detected falling into Saturn's equator ... less than 100 million years to live
contradictory_evidence: c08: a 2024 Nature Geoscience simulation argues the rings may be far older than their appearance suggests, which undercuts age estimates based on it.

claim: A 2024 simulation study argues Saturn's rings could be as old as the Solar System, about 4.5 billion years.
excerpt: could be as old as the Solar System (about 4.5 billions of years)
context: Hyodo, Madeira and Genda, Nature Geoscience, 16 December 2024. It concerns the rings' age; the ring-rain rate is a separate question.
contradictory_evidence: c07: the 2018 release finds the rings unlikely to be older than 100 million years.

claim: Ring boundaries and optical depths used in the render: C ring from 74,658 km, B ring 91,975 to 117,507 km, A ring 122,340 to 136,780 km.
excerpt: C ring inner edge 74,658; B ring inner edge 91,975; B ring outer edge 117,507; A ring inner edge 122,340; A ring outer edge 136,780

claim: A Saturn with no rings at all, shown in the final scene.
excerpt: less than 100 million years to live
context: Nobody has observed this. It extrapolates model c07, which c08 disputes. Labelled HYPOTHETICAL on screen.

claim: Render choices that are not data: field lines drawn as a centred dipole, grain size, count and speed, foreground ice chunks, planet colour grade, ring fine structure within sourced optical-depth ranges, gap widths, planet phases and enlarged planet markers.
excerpt: Saturn's magnetic field has significant quadrapole and octapole moments, making approximation of the central field as an offset dipole difficult.
context: The excerpt is why the dipole drawing is flagged: it is a simplification, not the measured field. The on-screen disclosure says every shot is a render.
